Beyond Trade Routes — Path Dependence and Institutional Overperformance in HRE Cities, 1200–1500

Data & analysis for the paper. Every figure exports to output/paper_figures/ and every table to output/paper_tables/.

1. Sample & Data

Headline. The analysis uses an unbalanced panel of 660 city-year observations across 225 cities in the HRE-centered Central European urban system, observed at century benchmarks from 1300 to 1500. Each observation has a 100-year-lagged Bairoch/Buringh population endpoint and six factor scores constructed at year T; the panel is unbalanced because not every city has both pop_T and pop_{T-100} in Buringh at every benchmark.

The panel uses Buringh's expanded urban-population dataset (Buringh 2021) as the primary outcome series. Buringh covers 2,262 European settlements at century snapshots (700, 800, ..., 1500, ..., 2000), with population in thousands plus transport-location classifications. We restrict to cities in the HRE and imperial-periphery urban zone — modern Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Czech Republic, Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg, and Slovenia (414 cities). This sample captures the HRE-centered Central European urban system, but we do not claim every Low-Countries or Bohemian city was politically inside the HRE in every year of the period; some cities sit on imperial peripheries whose status shifted. After spatial+name matching to the Bairoch city_id system used by our factor builders, 225 cities have both a population endpoint and at least one valid factor measurement and so enter the analysis.

The six factors at year T (state-of-the-city, 50-yr aggregations):

  • Legal capacity — formal charter, town hall, free-imperial / imperial / free-city status, distance to nearest pre-1500 university, legal-family code (Magdeburg, Lübeck, Kulm).
  • Merchant capital — Hanseatic membership, Viabundus fair tier (interregional / regional / local), staple rights, Bairoch-listed Messe presence, market attestation.
  • Trade access (geography) — Viabundus trade-route membership, fair density within 50 km, distance to navigable river or land road. Bairoch-keyed, with a Bairoch+south- German fallback so Augsburg, Ulm, Würzburg, Regensburg, Bamberg, Speyer, and Rothenburg are no longer zero by data artefact.
  • Agricultural surplus — Voronoi hinterland area, centuries-since-first-mention, river distance, latitude band, elevation. Population is intentionally NOT in this score (the prior version leaked the outcome).
  • Noble extraction (–) — terr_id transitions in the 50-yr window, foreign rule, prince-bishop seat. Higher = more lord-extraction.
  • Conflict risk (–) — number of conflict incidents, major sieges, fire-damage events in the 50-yr window.

1.1 What's missing on purpose (and why)

Peasant mobility is excluded from the regressions. The score (build_peasant_mobility.py) is constructed as a deterministic function of three other factors (legal capacity, merchant capital, noble extraction), so feeding it into the regression yields perfect collinearity. It is retained in the heuristic composite for narrative continuity but not estimated here.

2. The HRE Urban System: 1200 vs 1500

The first historical fact your paper needs to establish is what the HRE urban system looked like at the start versus the end of the period. These two maps use the same population threshold (≥ 2,000 inhabitants in Buringh) so they are directly comparable.

2.1 HRE 1200

Reading this figure

Each dot is one city; size and color encode population (log scale on color, linear on dot area). The 1200 map shows a sparse, mostly Rhine-and-Danube-corridor urban system — the bulk of large cities sit in the Rhineland (Cologne, Mainz, Worms, Speyer, Strasbourg) with secondary clusters in the Low Countries (Ghent, Bruges, Tournai), and a thin scattering across the rest of the empire. Most modern German towns either don't yet exist as cities or fall below the 2k threshold.

Use in the paper. Establish the "starting position" of the urban system in the Introduction (alongside a 1-paragraph summary). The dispersion-along-rivers pattern foreshadows the trade-access argument and motivates including river/route variables as controls.

2.2 HRE 1500

Reading this figure

Three centuries later, the urban system is denser everywhere. New large cities have appeared in the south (Augsburg, Nuremberg, Ulm), in central Germany (Erfurt, Magdeburg), and along the Baltic (Lübeck, Hamburg, Bremen, Danzig). The Rhine corridor is still dominant but no longer alone. The pattern of growth is geographically uneven — the north-east (Hanseatic League cities) and the south (free imperial cities of Swabia and Franconia) are the new additions.

Use in the paper. The visual contrast between this map and the 1200 map is your case for "city growth is heterogeneous — some regions filled in dramatically, others changed little." The residuals analysis in §4 explains why.

3. Path-Dependence Baseline (Model 1)

log(pop_T) = α + β_lag · log(pop_T-100) + γ_T · year_FE + ε

Plain English. "Given how big the city was 100 years ago, plus which year T is, predict its log population today. No other inputs."

n observations
660
225 cities × 3 years
In-sample R²
+0.742
fit on training data
5-fold CV R²
+0.729
± 0.072 (held-out cities)
β_lag (autocorrelation)
+0.898
95% CI [+0.862, +0.930]

The β_lag estimate is +0.898, with a 95% bootstrap CI of [+0.862, +0.930]. A coefficient near 1 means the city's log population at T is approximately a constant offset from log population at T-100 — i.e., growth rates are roughly common across cities and the rank-ordering by size is mostly preserved over a century. This is the path-dependence claim.

3.1 Calibration plot

Reading this figure

X-axis: actual log(pop_T). Y-axis: predicted log(pop_T) from the lag-only model. Each dot is one (city, year) observation; the dashed line is y = x (perfect prediction). Color encodes year T.

The cloud is tight against the y = x line and centered on it, which means the lag term alone gets within a factor of e0.3 ≈ 1.35× of actual population for most cities. That single coefficient explains R² ≈ 0.73 of the cross-sectional variance — by far the dominant force in the data.

Use in the paper. This is your headline finding's first half: path dependence dominated. Lead Section 6 (Results) with this plot.

4. Residuals — Who Beat Expectations?

From Model 1 we get a residual for every city-year observation:

residual_T = log(pop_T) − [α̂ + β̂_lag · log(pop_T-100) + γ̂_T]

Cities with positive residuals grew (or shrank less) more than their inherited trajectory predicted. Cities with negative residuals fell short of their inherited trajectory. The mean residual is by construction near zero; what matters is the geographic, factor-driven structure in the residuals.

4.1 Distribution of residuals

Reading this figure

The residuals are roughly bell-shaped and centered on zero. Spread is ~0.3 log-points per side, meaning the typical city's actual log population deviates from the lag-only prediction by ~0.3 — which on the population scale is roughly ±35%.

4.2 Geographic distribution of residuals

Reading this figure

This is the most diagnostic plot in the paper. Red = beat its inherited trajectory, blue = fell short. The colorbar shows residual = actual − predicted; positive residuals (red) are cities larger than the lag-only model expects. Top over/under-performers are labeled. Watch for spatial clustering:

  • Concentrations of red identify regions where something pushed cities to grow faster than path dependence alone suggests.
  • Concentrations of blue are regions where cities underperformed — usually because of conflict, lord extraction, or shifting trade routes.
  • If the colors are random with no spatial pattern, the residual is mostly idiosyncratic noise — and your factors will struggle to explain it.

Use in the paper. Pair this map with §5 to make the institutional-overperformance argument concrete.

5. What Predicts Overperformance? (Model 2)

residual_T = α + Σ β_k · z(factor_k_at_T) + γ_T · year_FE + ε

Plain English. "Among cities that started at the same size, which institutional and geographic factors predict who exceeded the inherited trajectory?"

R² of residuals on factors
+0.050
incremental over Model 1
5-fold CV R²
+0.021
± 0.027

Note that the headline R² for this regression is small. That is expected and correct: most of the variance in city size was already explained by lag pop in Model 1. Model 2 is asking only about the residual variance — what's left after the dominant force is removed. Even small significant coefficients here are doing real explanatory work.

5.1 Coefficient plot

Reading this figure

Each bar is a factor's β coefficient. Bars to the right of zero mean the factor predicts positive residuals (beat trajectory). Black whiskers are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Green bars exclude zero on the positive side (significantly increases overperformance); red bars exclude zero on the negative side; gray bars cross zero (insufficient evidence to claim a sign).

Read these as: per +1 standard deviation increase in this factor at year T (holding other factors fixed), the residual changes by β log-points. β = +0.10 means cities one SD above average on this factor are typically e0.10 ≈ 10.5% larger than what lag pop alone would predict.

Factor (z-scored, +1 SD)β on residual95% CISig.
Legal capacity+0.0789[+0.0475, +0.1137]significant
Merchant capital+0.0577[+0.0229, +0.0853]significant
Trade access-0.0124[-0.0449, +0.0240]not significant
Agricultural surplus-0.0384[-0.0734, -0.0100]significant
Noble extraction (–)+0.0242[-0.0126, +0.0593]not significant

The factors that survive a 95% CI test of "this matters above and beyond path dependence" are the ones to lead with in your Results section. Insignificant factors are still worth mentioning — they tell you what does not drive overperformance once starting size is controlled.

Interpreting the agricultural-surplus coefficient

The agricultural-surplus proxy is negative and statistically significant in Model 2. Be careful with this result in the paper. The proxy combines hinterland Voronoi area, river distance, elevation, latitude band, and centuries-since- first-mention — all geographic/structural inputs, but none of which directly measure agricultural output. The defensible reading is:

"After controlling for inherited city size and institutional-commercial factors, the agricultural-surplus proxy is negatively associated with overperformance, suggesting that urban takeoff was less about rural carrying capacity alone and more about institutional-commercial concentration."

Avoid the simpler claim "agricultural surplus hurt city growth" — the data cannot support it, and the proxy is likely picking up cities whose growth was bottlenecked by other factors despite favourable hinterland geography.

5.3 Priority cities — residual trajectories

Reading this figure

Each line is one priority city; X = year, Y = residual at that year. A line above zero means the city was beating its trajectory at that benchmark; below zero means falling short. Trajectories that climb over time are cities that compounded overperformance (institutional flywheel); trajectories that fall are cities whose advantage decayed.

This is the right figure to put next to your case-study section — it lets you point at, e.g., Leipzig's late-15th-century rise or Erfurt's ceiling-effect under Mainz overlordship.

7. Geographic Determinants (Buringh transport-location)

Buringh classifies every city by its access to a major water-catchment system or land route. The classes are: river [north/baltic/black/ mediterranean] sea, land [north/baltic/atlantic/etc.], north sea + river, baltic + river, etc. This is a much sharper geographic feature than Bairoch supplies.

Reading this figure (descriptive only)

Each line is one transport class; markers at 1300/1400/1500 show the mean log(pop) of cities in that class at each benchmark. Steeper-rising lines = classes whose cities grew faster on average.

Treat this as a descriptive supplement, not a statistical claim. Several classes have very small sample sizes — e.g., "north sea + river" and "baltic + river" each have only 3–5 HRE cities. Differences between classes with such small n are not formally identified.

The descriptive pattern: cities combining sea access with inland river penetration (Hamburg, Bremen, Lübeck) sit in the highest-mean classes; pure inland-land classes sit lower. Bosker & Buringh (2017) "City seeds" argue physical geography and transport access were the original "city seeds."

Recommended phrasing for the paper: "Transport location mattered descriptively, but the residual model suggests that institutional and merchant capacity better explain which cities outperformed."

8. Robustness: Buringh vs Bairoch

Reading this figure

Each dot is a city-year observation. X = log(Buringh pop), Y = log(Bairoch pop). The dashed line is y = x. The Pearson r in the title quantifies how closely the two datasets agree.

Tight clustering around y = x means the two datasets are essentially the same data with minor revisions; your conclusions are robust to which one you use as the outcome. Systematic deviation (e.g., Buringh consistently higher) would signal a coverage or coding difference that needs a footnote.

Use in the paper. Footnote in §4 (Data) — "All results are robust to using Buringh's expanded panel; r between sources is X for matched cities."

9. Implications for the Paper

The two-sentence finding. HRE city size was overwhelmingly path-dependent: cities that were big in year T-100 were big in year T (β_lag ≈ 0.90, R² ≈ 0.73). Among cities that started at the same size, those with stronger Legal capacity, Merchant capital exceeded their inherited trajectory.

9.1 What this lets you claim

  • Path dependence is the first-order story — and this is itself a contribution, since most of the literature treats institutions or trade routes as the primary cause of urban growth. Your main result repositions them as explaining deviation, not levels.
  • Within-cohort heterogeneity is what institutions explain. When you control for starting size, the factors that survive the 95% CI test are the institutional / commercial-capacity ones. That is the quantitative version of the Cantoni–Yuchtman story.
  • The HRE's fragmentation matters here precisely because it generated wide variation in legal status, rulers, and commercial privileges. A more unified state (e.g., the French crown's centralization) would have given less variation in these factors and thus a tighter, less informative residual.

9.2 What this does NOT let you claim

  • That you have identified a causal channel — these are observational regressions, and the factors are themselves outcomes of the same political processes that produced city growth. The paper should be careful with the word "cause".
  • That the model would forecast 1500–1600. Temporal extrapolation across regime shifts is a documented failure of this model (the 1400→1500 holdout in our earlier predictive-model report had R² < 0).

9.3 Recommended paper structure (your reframe)

  1. Introduction — open with the 1200 vs 1500 maps; state the puzzle (heterogeneous urban growth despite shared political environment).
  2. Historical background — HRE fragmentation, urban autonomy, charters, fairs, prince-bishops.
  3. Literature — Bairoch / Buringh on data; Cantoni–Yuchtman on markets and universities; Bosker & Buringh "city seeds" on geography; Bosker–Buringh–van Zanden on institutions.
  4. Data — describe panel construction, factor definitions, missingness; Buringh vs Bairoch robustness.
  5. Empirical strategy — Model 1 (path-dependence baseline) and Model 2 (residual on factors). Justify why this is the right specification (avoids tautological R²; isolates within-cohort heterogeneity).
  6. Results — lead with Model 1 (path dependence dominates). Then Model 2 (institutions explain residuals).
  7. Case studies — pick 3–4 of the priority cities whose residual trajectories illustrate the mechanism.
  8. Conclusion — return to the main claim; note limits and avenues for future work.
